From the previous analysis, only cases 3 (b becomes c then d) and 4 (a becomes b then a) contain a chained replacement. "abcde" contains both a and b, so both cases show the wrong output.

Answer: 3 and 4 only

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

The flaw: a character already replaced can be replaced again later in the j loop, if newc[j] equals a later oldc[k] (k [latex]\gt[/latex] j).

- (1) abc[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]dab: b[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a, but a comes earlier in oldc [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] no chain
- (2) cde[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]bcd: no chain
- (3) bca[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]cda: b[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]c, then c[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]d [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] flaw shown
- (4) abc[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]bac: a[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]b, then b[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] flaw shown

Answer: Only two
